endorsements.quote: To improve accuracy, developers must conduct rigorous, representative testing across diverse populations before releasing mental health tools.

For example, mental health assessment apps should be tested for diagnostic reliability across different racial, gender, and socioeconomic groups to ensure consistent performance regardless of user identity.

A human-centric mental health app could involve participatory design practices, where individuals with lived mental health experiences are directly involved in shaping features, user interfaces, and accessibility options.
For instance, integrating customizable settings to accommodate users with disabilities ensures that technology adapts to users rather than forcing users to adapt to the technology.
To uphold privacy, mental health platforms must implement strong data encryption and clear consent protocols.
Potential solutions include model cards and data cards to detail how AI-driven recommendations are generated [ 46 ], as well as structured reporting guidelines for research involving LLMs [ 47 ].
Doing so will best support age-appropriate education about AI-enabled large language models and their mental health implications across all levels of community engagement.
Where possible, users should have control over their data [ 41 ].

unlisted_practices: Disclose to users when they are interacting with an AI system versus a human professional.
Clarify to users how their personal data is used to shape AI responses.
Use federated learning so user data remain on local devices rather than centralized servers.
Provide transparent data-sharing options so users control who accesses their sensitive information.
Translate technical transparency information into forms understandable and meaningful to users.
Offer tiered pricing models or subsidized access to make digital mental health tools affordable.
Provide language accessibility in digital health tools.
Conduct outreach to low-income and underserved populations for participation in pilot programs.
Involve youth through advisory boards, participatory design, and youth-led advocacy in developing mental health technologies.
Ensure diverse representation in product development and clinical trials of neurotechnologies.
Invest in community-engaged research and design culturally responsive technologies.
Fund mental health initiatives in underserved communities and expand internet access and digital infrastructure.
Engage policymakers to enforce legal protections and regulations for neurotechnology.
Build a rigorous evidence base on AI and youth mental health that addresses methodological shortcomings of earlier research on digital harms.
Examine who develops, trains, and deploys AI models and how their perspectives and power dynamics influence model behavior and harms.

screen.reason: This is a perspective/framework article reporting on principles and guardrails for deploying AI/LLM chatbots in youth digital mental health resulting from an interdisciplinary workshop.
